title: Ἀντίλοχος καὶ Ἕκτωρ
titleEn: The Fall of Melanippus and Hector’s Charge — Iliad 15.559–652
part: The Fall of Melanippus and Hector’s Charge (15.559–652)
about: Ajax calls on the Argives to be men and to respect one another, and they fence the ships with a bronze bulwark while Zeus rouses the Trojans. Menelaus urges young Antilochus to leap out and hit a Trojan, and Antilochus kills Melanippus, then gives ground before Hector like a beast that has killed a dog or a herdsman, and stands again when he reaches his companions. The poet turns to the plan of Zeus: Hector is to set a ship on fire, so that Thetis’ prayer is fulfilled and the Trojans are driven back from the ships. Zeus honours Hector, whose life is short, since Athena is already bringing on his day at the hands of Achilles. Hector rages like fire and strikes at the Achaean line, which stands like a rock against the sea; he falls on it like a wave on a ship and like a lion among cattle, and kills Periphetes of Mycenae, who trips on his own shield; his companions cannot help him, for they fear Hector.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν ἦρχ’, ὃ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕσπετο ἰσόθεος φώς·
sentences.l: So having spoken, the one led the way, and the other followed along, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: So he spoke and led the way, and the other followed with him, a man the equal of a god.
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν … ὃ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’, the old pronoun use of the article: the first is Hector, who has just finished speaking at the end of the last part, and the second is Melanippus, the man he was rebuking. ἦρχ’ is ἦρχε, from ἄρχω ‘lead the way’, and ἕσπετο is a past tense of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, with ἅμ’ (= ἅμα) ‘along with’. ἰσόθεος φώς ‘a man equal to a god’ is a stock phrase, translated every time; φώς with this accent is ‘man’, a different word from φῶς ‘light’.

sentences.t: Ἀργείους δ’ ὄτρυνε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l: And the Argives he urged on, great Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: Great Telamonian Ajax urged on the Argives:
sentences.n: Ἀργείους is the object, put first, and the subject comes last: μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας ‘great Telamonian Ajax’, the stock name-and-epithet phrase, where Τελαμώνιος tells this Ajax, the son of Telamon, from the other Ajax, the son of Oileus. ὄτρυνε is a past tense of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, with no augment. The line ends with a raised stop where English puts a colon, and the speech follows. The edition prints no quotation marks, and the English adds them.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι ἀνέρες ἔστε, καὶ αἰδῶ θέσθ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
ἀλλήλους τ’ αἰδεῖσθε κατὰ κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας.
sentences.l:
“Friends, be men, and put shame in your heart,
and respect one another through the strong battles.
sentences.i: “Friends, be men, and put shame in your hearts, and respect one another throughout the strong battles.
sentences.n: Ajax speaks. ὦ φίλοι ‘friends’ is a vocative, ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ, and ἔστε is the imperative of εἰμί: ‘be men’. θέσθ’ is the aorist middle imperative of τίθημι, ‘put for yourselves’, and αἰδῶ is the accusative of αἰδώς ‘shame’, the sense of what others will think of you; ἐνὶ is ἐν, and θυμῷ is the dative of θυμός. αἰδεῖσθε is the imperative of αἰδέομαι ‘respect’, and κρατερὰς ὑσμίνας ‘strong battles’ is a stock phrase, translated every time. The second line is word for word 5.530.

sentences.t: αἰδομένων δ’ ἀνδρῶν πλέονες σόοι ἠὲ πέφανται·
sentences.l: And of men who feel respect more are safe than have been slain;
sentences.i: And of men who feel respect, more are safe than are slain;
sentences.n: αἰδομένων ἀνδρῶν ‘of men who feel respect’ is a genitive of the group from which the count is made, with αἰδομένων the present participle of αἰδέομαι, the verb of the line before. πλέονες is the epic form of πλείονες ‘more’, and σόοι the epic form of σῶοι ‘safe’. ἠέ ‘than’ follows the comparative, and πέφανται is the perfect passive of φένω ‘slay’, ‘have been slain’, a different word from φαίνω ‘show’. The line is 5.531 with δ’ added, which the English renders ‘and’.

sentences.t: φευγόντων δ’ οὔτ’ ἂρ κλέος ὄρνυται οὔτέ τις ἀλκή.
sentences.l: but of men who flee neither glory arises, nor any might.”
sentences.i: but when men flee, no glory rises up for them, nor any might.”
sentences.n: φευγόντων ‘of men who flee’ is a genitive in the same pattern as the line before, now for the opposite outcome. οὔτ’ ἂρ … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’. ὄρνυται is the present middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, here ‘arises’, and ἀλκή is the strength to defend oneself, ‘might’. The line has the words of 5.532. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀλέξασθαι μενέαινον,
ἐν θυμῷ δ’ ἐβάλοντο ἔπος, φράξαντο δὲ νῆας
ἕρκεϊ χαλκείῳ·
sentences.i: So he spoke; they were already eager to defend themselves, and they laid his word up in their hearts, and fenced the ships with a bronze bulwark;
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ καὶ αὐτοί ‘and they themselves also’ says the Argives were already eager before Ajax spoke. ἀλέξασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, ‘defend oneself’, and μενέαινον the imperfect of μενεαίνω ‘be eager’. ἐβάλοντο is the aorist middle of βάλλω; ἐν θυμῷ … ἔπος ἐβάλοντο is ‘laid the word up in their heart’. φράξαντο is the aorist middle of φράσσω ‘fence in’. ἕρκεϊ χαλκείῳ ‘with a bronze fence’ is a dative of means; a fence of bronze is not a built wall, and the Greek does not say what it is.

sentences.t: ἐπὶ δὲ Ζεὺς Τρῶας ἔγειρεν.
sentences.l: and against them Zeus was rousing the Trojans.
sentences.i: while Zeus was rousing the Trojans against them.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ stands alone as an adverb, ‘upon them, against them’, since Τρῶας is the object of ἔγειρεν. ἔγειρεν is the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’, so the rousing goes on while the Argives make their fence. This is the first mention of Zeus in the part; the lines from 592 on say what he intends.

sentences.t: Ἀντίλοχον δ’ ὄτρυνε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.l: And Antilochus he urged on, Menelaus, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Menelaus, good at the war-cry, urged on Antilochus:
sentences.n: Ἀντίλοχον is the object, put first as Ἀργείους was at 560, and the subject follows: βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος ‘Menelaus, good at the war-cry’, a stock epithet, translated every time, where βοήν ‘shout, war-cry’ is an accusative of respect. Antilochus is the son of Nestor, named so at 589. A speech follows. ὄτρυνε is the same past tense as at 560.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’ οὔ τις σεῖο νεώτερος ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν,
οὔτε ποσὶν θάσσων οὔτ’ ἄλκιμος ὡς σὺ μάχεσθαι·
sentences.l:
“Antilochus, no one is younger than you, no other of the Achaeans,
neither swifter on foot nor valiant as you are at fighting;
sentences.i: “Antilochus, no other of the Achaeans is younger than you, nor swifter on foot, nor as valiant as you in fighting;
sentences.n: Menelaus speaks. Ἀντίλοχ’ is the vocative. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ and goes with the comparative νεώτερος ‘younger’, ‘than you’; ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν is ‘other of the Achaeans’. θάσσων is the irregular comparative of ταχύς ‘swift’, with ποσίν ‘on foot’ (dative of respect). ἄλκιμος is ‘valiant’, ὡς σύ ‘as you (are)’, and μάχεσθαι an infinitive of respect, ‘at fighting’. The two οὔτε join the two qualities, and the whole sentence leads to the wish in the next line.

sentences.t: εἴ τινά που Τρώων ἐξάλμενος ἄνδρα βάλοισθα.
sentences.l: if some man of the Trojans, perhaps, having leapt out, you might hit.”
sentences.i: if only you might leap out and perhaps hit some man of the Trojans.”
sentences.n: εἰ with the optative βάλοισθα (aorist, second singular, in -σθα) is a wish whose main clause is left unsaid: ‘if only you might …’. ἐξάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐξάλλομαι ‘leap out’, which the next lines act out (ἐκ δ’ ἔθορε), and που softens the wish to ‘perhaps’. τινά … ἄνδρα is ‘some man’ and Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὃ μὲν αὖτις ἀπέσσυτο, τὸν δ’ ὀρόθυνεν·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he for his part rushed away again, and him he roused;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he rushed away again, but Antilochus he roused;
sentences.n: The speech is over. ὃ μὲν … τὸν δ’ ‘he … him’ sets Menelaus against Antilochus: Menelaus hurries off again (αὖτις), and Antilochus is the one he has roused. ἀπέσσυτο is a past tense of ἀποσεύομαι ‘rush away’ (σεύομαι with a doubled σ), and ὀρόθυνεν a past tense of ὀροθύνω ‘rouse, spur on’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἔθορε προμάχων, καὶ ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
ἀμφὶ ἓ παπτήνας·
sentences.l:
He leapt out from the front-fighters, and cast with a shining spear,
having looked about him;
sentences.i: He leapt out from among the foremost fighters and, after looking about him, cast with his shining spear;
sentences.n: The subject, Antilochus, is not named again in the Greek. ἔθορε is the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and ἐκ … προμάχων ‘out from the front-fighters’ has the preverb set apart from its noun. ἀκόντισε ‘cast’ has no object yet; it comes at 576. δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’, and ἀμφὶ ἓ παπτήνας ‘having looked about him’ (ἕ is the reflexive, παπτήνας the aorist participle of παπταίνω). The second half of 573 and all of 574 are also said of Odysseus at 4.496–497.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δὲ Τρῶες κεκάδοντο
ἀνδρὸς ἀκοντίσσαντος·
sentences.l:
and back the Trojans drew away
before the man who had cast;
sentences.i: and the Trojans drew back before the man who had cast his spear;
sentences.n: κεκάδοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of χάζομαι ‘give way, draw back’, and ὑπό, set apart from its verb, is ‘back, away’. ἀνδρὸς ἀκοντίσσαντος is ‘the man having cast’, the aorist participle of ἀκοντίζω with a doubled σ for the metre, in the genitive either as a genitive absolute or as the one they gave way before; the sense is the same. These words are word for word 4.497–498.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οὐχ ἅλιον βέλος ἧκεν,
ἀλλ’ Ἱκετάονος υἱὸν ὑπέρθυμον Μελάνιππον
νισόμενον πόλεμον δὲ βάλε στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν.
sentences.l:
and he did not send a shaft in vain,
but Hicetaon’s son, high-spirited Melanippus,
as he was going to the war, he hit in the chest beside the nipple.
sentences.i: He did not send his shaft in vain, but hit the son of Hicetaon, high-spirited Melanippus, as he was going to the war, in the chest beside the nipple.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Antilochus. ἅλιον ‘in vain’ is a different word from ἅλιος ‘of the sea’; βέλος is a ‘shaft’, any missile; and ἧκεν is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’. Ἱκετάονος is the epic genitive of Ἱκετάων, and ὑπέρθυμον ‘high-spirited’ a stock epithet. Melanippus is the man Hector rebuked in the last part. νισόμενον is the present participle of νίσομαι ‘go’, and πόλεμον δέ is ‘to the war’, with the suffix -δε of direction. στῆθος παρὰ μαζόν is ‘in the chest beside the nipple’.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν.
sentences.l: And he fell with a thud, and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: He fell with a thud, and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω ‘thud’, the heavy sound of a body falling, and πεσών is ‘having fallen’. The second half of the line is a death formula that also stands at 4.461: τὸν … ὄσσε are both accusative (‘him … his eyes’), and ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’. σκότος is ‘darkness’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἐπόρουσε κύων ὥς, ὅς τ’ ἐπὶ νεβρῷ
βλημένῳ ἀΐξῃ, τόν τ’ ἐξ εὐνῆφι θορόντα
θηρητὴρ ἐτύχησε βαλών, ὑπέλυσε δὲ γυῖα·
sentences.i: Antilochus rushed on like a dog that darts upon a fawn already struck, which a hunter has hit with his cast as it leapt from its lair, and has loosened its limbs;
sentences.n: κύων ὥς ‘like a dog’ opens a simile, and ὅς τ’ … ἀΐξῃ (aorist subjunctive of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’) is its general relative clause. νεβρῷ βλημένῳ is ‘a fawn that has been struck’ (the epic aorist middle participle of βάλλω, passive in sense). ἐξ εὐνῆφι has the old ending -φι: ‘out of the lair’. θορόντα is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, ἐτύχησε is ‘hit’, and βαλών ‘by casting’. ὑπέλυσε δὲ γυῖα ‘and loosened its limbs’ is the Homeric idiom for killing, and ὑπό adds ‘from beneath’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐπὶ σοὶ Μελάνιππε θόρ’ Ἀντίλοχος μενεχάρμης
τεύχεα συλήσων·
sentences.l:
So upon you, Melanippus, leapt Antilochus, steadfast in the fray,
intending to strip your armour;
sentences.i: So, Melanippus, Antilochus, steadfast in the fray, leapt upon you to strip your armour;
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile and turns to Melanippus, addressed in the vocative (Μελάνιππε), who is already dead. ἐπὶ σοί is ‘upon you’, and θόρ’ is the aorist of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, the verb of the simile again. μενεχάρμης ‘steadfast in the fray’ is a stock epithet, translated every time. συλήσων is the future participle of συλάω ‘strip’, and states the purpose: ‘to strip’ the armour, τεύχεα.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ λάθεν Ἕκτορα δῖον,
ὅς ῥά οἱ ἀντίος ἦλθε θέων ἀνὰ δηϊοτῆτα.
sentences.l:
but he did not escape heavenly Hector,
who then came opposite him, running through the fighting.
sentences.i: but he did not escape the notice of heavenly Hector, who came running through the fighting to face him.
sentences.n: λάθεν is the unaugmented aorist of λανθάνω, which takes an accusative: ‘escape the notice of’ Hector. The subject, ‘he’, is Antilochus, and Ἕκτορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hector’ is the stock phrase. ὅς ῥά οἱ ἀντίος ἦλθε is ‘who came opposite him’: ὅς is the relative, ῥα a particle of lively narrative, οἱ ‘to him’ and ἀντίος ‘facing’. θέων is the participle of θέω ‘run’, and ἀνὰ δηϊοτῆτα ‘through the fighting’ has the accusative of δηϊοτής.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ οὐ μεῖνε θοός περ ἐὼν πολεμιστής,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἄρ’ ἔτρεσε θηρὶ κακὸν ῥέξαντι ἐοικώς,
ὅς τε κύνα κτείνας ἢ βουκόλον ἀμφὶ βόεσσι
φεύγει πρίν περ ὅμιλον ἀολλισθήμεναι ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
But Antilochus did not stand fast, swift though being a warrior,
but he then took fright, like a beast that has done evil,
which, having killed a dog or a cowherd about the cattle,
flees even before a throng of men has gathered together;
sentences.i: But Antilochus, swift warrior though he was, did not hold his ground; he took fright like a beast that has done evil, which, after killing a dog or a cowherd by the cattle, flees even before a throng of men has gathered together;
sentences.n: μεῖνε is the aorist of μένω, with no object ‘stand firm’; θοός περ ἐὼν πολεμιστής is ‘swift though being a warrior’, with concessive περ. ἔτρεσε is the aorist of τρέω ‘take fright, flee in fear’. θηρὶ κακὸν ῥέξαντι ἐοικώς is ‘like a beast that has done evil’: ῥέξαντι is the aorist participle of ῥέζω, and ἐοικώς, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, takes the dative. ὅς τε is a general relative, and ἀμφὶ βόεσσι ‘about the cattle’. ἀολλισθήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of ἀολλίζω ‘gather together’.

sentences.t:
ὣς τρέσε Νεστορίδης, ἐπὶ δὲ Τρῶές τε καὶ Ἕκτωρ
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ βέλεα στονόεντα χέοντο·
sentences.l:
So took fright the son of Nestor, and after him the Trojans and Hector
with wondrous din poured missiles full of groaning;
sentences.i: So the son of Nestor took fright, and after him the Trojans and Hector poured missiles that brought groaning, with a wondrous din;
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile. τρέσε is the same aorist as ἔτρεσε at 586, without the augment. Νεστορίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Nestor’, for Antilochus. ἐπὶ δέ … is ‘and after him’, with ἐπί as an adverb, and χέοντο is the imperfect middle of χέω ‘pour’. ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ is ‘with a wondrous din’, a dative of manner, and βέλεα στονόεντα ‘missiles full of groaning’ come from στόνος ‘groan’.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ μεταστρεφθείς, ἐπεὶ ἵκετο ἔθνος ἑταίρων.
sentences.l: And he stood, having turned about, when he reached the company of his companions.
sentences.i: He turned about and stood when he reached the company of his companions.
sentences.n: The subject is Antilochus. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, without the augment, and μεταστρεφθείς is the aorist passive participle of μεταστρέφω ‘turn about’. ἐπεὶ ἵκετο ‘when he reached’ has the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι. ἔθνος ἑταίρων ‘the company of his companions’ is a phrase the poet uses of a group of one’s own side.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ λείουσιν ἐοικότες ὠμοφάγοισι
νηυσὶν ἐπεσσεύοντο, Διὸς δ’ ἐτέλειον ἐφετμάς,
ὅ σφισιν αἰὲν ἔγειρε μένος μέγα, θέλγε δὲ θυμὸν
Ἀργείων καὶ κῦδος ἀπαίνυτο, τοὺς δ’ ὀρόθυνεν.
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, like raw-eating lions,
rushed on at the ships, and were fulfilling the commands of Zeus,
who was ever rousing great might in them, and was enchanting the heart
of the Argives, and taking glory away, and them he roused.
sentences.i: The Trojans, like lions that eat raw flesh, rushed on at the ships and were fulfilling the commands of Zeus, who kept rousing great might in them, and was enchanting the heart of the Argives and taking glory away from them, while the Trojans he roused.
sentences.n: λείουσιν ἐοικότες ὠμοφάγοισι is ‘like raw-eating lions’: λείουσιν is the epic dative plural of λέων, and ὠμοφάγοισι means ‘eating raw flesh’. ἐπεσσεύοντο is the imperfect of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’, with νηυσίν ‘at the ships’. ἐτέλειον is the imperfect of τελέω ‘fulfil’. In what follows ὅ is the pronoun ‘he’, Zeus; σφισιν is ‘in them’, the Trojans; θέλγε ‘enchanted’ and κῦδος ἀπαίνυτο ‘took glory away’ are said of the Argives; and τοὺς δ’ ‘and these’ are the Trojans again.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορι γάρ οἱ θυμὸς ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι
Πριαμίδῃ, ἵνα νηυσὶ κορωνίσι θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ
ἐμβάλοι ἀκάματον, Θέτιδος δ’ ἐξαίσιον ἀρὴν
πᾶσαν ἐπικρήνειε·
sentences.i: for his heart wished to grant glory to Hector, son of Priam, so that Hector might hurl untiring, wondrous-blazing fire upon the curved ships, and Zeus bring the whole of Thetis’ outrageous prayer to fulfilment;
sentences.n: Zeus is still the subject, and οἱ θυμός is ‘his heart’. ὀρέξαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀρέγω ‘grant’, and Πριαμίδῃ ‘Priam’s son’ is a patronymic for Hector. ἵνα begins a purpose clause with two optatives: ἐμβάλοι, of Hector, takes θεσπιδαὲς πῦρ ‘wondrous-blazing fire’, with ἀκάματον ‘untiring’ set after the verb, and ἐπικρήνειε, of Zeus, ‘fulfil’ (ἐπικραίνω). The Greek does not mark the change of subject. ἐξαίσιον ‘outrageous’ is from ἐξ + αἶσα ‘portion’, ‘beyond what is allotted’; the prayer is one Thetis made to Zeus earlier in the poem, and this part does not repeat it.

sentences.t:
τὸ γὰρ μένε μητίετα Ζεὺς
νηὸς καιομένης σέλας ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
for this counsellor Zeus was awaiting,
the blaze of a burning ship to see with his eyes.
sentences.i: for this was what Zeus the counsellor was waiting for: to see with his eyes the blaze of a burning ship.
sentences.n: τὸ γὰρ μένε: τό is the object of μένε, the unaugmented imperfect of μένω ‘wait for’, and γάρ gives the reason for the plan. μητίετα Ζεύς is ‘Zeus the counsellor’, with μητίετα, a stock epithet, translated every time. The infinitive ἰδέσθαι ‘to see’ says what he is waiting for, and its object is σέλας ‘blaze’, with νηὸς καιομένης ‘of a burning ship’, singular. ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘with his eyes’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ γὰρ δὴ τοῦ μέλλε παλίωξιν παρὰ νηῶν
θησέμεναι Τρώων, Δαναοῖσι δὲ κῦδος ὀρέξειν.
sentences.l:
for from that time he was going to make a chase back from beside the ships
of the Trojans, and to the Danaans to grant glory.
sentences.i: For from that time on he was going to bring about a chase back of the Trojans from beside the ships, and to grant glory to the Danaans.
sentences.n: ἐκ δὴ τοῦ is ‘from that point on’, that is, from the burning of the ship. μέλλε (the unaugmented ἔμελλε) with the future infinitives θησέμεναι (epic -μεναι, from τίθημι) and ὀρέξειν ‘was going to put’ and ‘to grant’ states what Zeus has fixed. παλίωξις is a rare word, from πάλιν ‘back’ and a root meaning ‘chase’, and ‘a chase back’ is the traditional sense; its exact sense is not known. Τρώων is the genitive of the people chased back. Δαναοῖσι is the epic dative plural, ‘to the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
τὰ φρονέων νήεσσιν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἔγειρεν
Ἕκτορα Πριαμίδην μάλα περ μεμαῶτα καὶ αὐτόν.
sentences.l:
Thinking these things, at the hollow ships he was rousing
Hector, Priam’s-son, though very eager even of himself.
sentences.i: With this in mind he was rousing Hector, son of Priam, at the hollow ships, very eager as he was already himself.
sentences.n: τὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking these things’, the plan just told. νήεσσιν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν is ‘at the hollow ships’, with ἔπι (= ἐπί) set after the noun it governs, the epic dative plural νήεσσιν and the stock γλαφυρῇσιν ‘hollow’. ἔγειρεν is the imperfect of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’. μεμαῶτα is the perfect participle of μέμονα ‘be eager’, and μάλα περ … καὶ αὐτόν says Hector was very eager already, ‘even of himself’.

sentences.t:
μαίνετο δ’ ὡς ὅτ’ Ἄρης ἐγχέσπαλος ἢ ὀλοὸν πῦρ
οὔρεσι μαίνηται βαθέης ἐν τάρφεσιν ὕλης·
sentences.l:
And he raged, as when spear-brandishing Ares, or deadly fire,
rages in the mountains in the thickets of a deep forest;
sentences.i: He raged as spear-brandishing Ares rages, or as deadly fire rages in the mountains, in the thickets of a deep forest;
sentences.n: μαίνετο is the imperfect of μαίνομαι ‘rage’, and the simile uses the same verb, μαίνηται, in the subjunctive after ὡς ὅτ’ ‘as when’. ἐγχέσπαλος is ‘spear-brandishing’ (ἔγχος ‘spear’, with a second element of uncertain formation); ὀλοὸν πῦρ is ‘deadly fire’. οὔρεσι is the epic form of ὄρεσι, ‘in the mountains’. τάρφεσιν is the dative plural of τάρφος ‘thicket’, and βαθέης … ὕλης ‘of a deep forest’ has the epic feminine genitive in -έης.

sentences.t:
ἀφλοισμὸς δὲ περὶ στόμα γίγνετο, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
λαμπέσθην βλοσυρῇσιν ὑπ’ ὀφρύσιν, ἀμφὶ δὲ πήληξ
σμερδαλέον κροτάφοισι τινάσσετο μαρναμένοιο
Ἕκτορος·
sentences.l:
And a foaming came about his mouth, and his two eyes
shone beneath grim brows, and about him the helmet
terribly on the temples was shaken of fighting
Hector;
sentences.i: Foam gathered about his mouth, his two eyes shone beneath his grim brows, and the helmet shook terribly about the temples of Hector as he fought;
sentences.n: ἀφλοισμός is ‘foaming’ and γίγνετο ‘came to be’. τὼ … ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’, and λαμπέσθην the dual imperfect of λάμπομαι ‘shine’. βλοσυρῇσιν ὑπ’ ὀφρύσιν is ‘beneath grim brows’; the exact sense of βλοσυρός is not certain, and ‘grim’ is the usual guess. πήληξ is ‘helmet’, τινάσσετο ‘was shaken’, and κροτάφοισι ‘on the temples’ is dative of place. μαρναμένοιο Ἕκτορος ‘of fighting Hector’ is a genitive that goes with κροτάφοισι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς γάρ οἱ ἀπ’ αἰθέρος ἦεν ἀμύντωρ
Ζεύς, ὅς μιν πλεόνεσσι μετ’ ἀνδράσι μοῦνον ἐόντα
τίμα καὶ κύδαινε.
sentences.i: For Zeus himself was his defender from the upper air, and honoured him and gave him glory, alone as he was among so many more men.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς … Ζεύς is ‘Zeus himself’, with ἀμύντωρ ‘defender’ as the predicate and οἱ ‘for him’ Hector. ἀπ’ αἰθέρος is ‘from the aether’, the bright upper air. μιν is ‘him’; πλεόνεσσι μετ’ ἀνδράσι is ‘among more men’, the epic dative plural of πλείων, and μοῦνον ἐόντα ‘being alone’ shows Hector outnumbered. τίμα and κύδαινε are imperfects; κύδαινε comes from κῦδος ‘glory’.

sentences.t:
μινυνθάδιος γὰρ ἔμελλεν
ἔσσεσθ’·
sentences.l:
for short-lived he was going
to be;
sentences.i: for he was going to be short-lived;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason Zeus honours Hector now: his life will be short. μινυνθάδιος is ‘short-lived’. ἔμελλεν with ἔσσεσθ’ (= ἔσσεσθαι, the epic future infinitive of εἰμί) is ‘was going to be’, as with μέλλε at 601, which has no augment.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ οἱ ἐπόρνυε μόρσιμον ἦμαρ
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη ὑπὸ Πηλεΐδαο βίηφιν.
sentences.l:
for already for him was rousing the allotted day
Pallas Athena, under the might of Peleus’-son.
sentences.i: for Pallas Athena was already bringing on his allotted day, by the might of the son of Peleus.
sentences.n: ἐπόρνυε is the imperfect of ἐπόρνυμι ‘rouse, bring on’, and μόρσιμον ἦμαρ is ‘the allotted day’, the day of Hector’s death; the subject, Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη ‘Pallas Athena’, comes last in the sentence. Πηλεΐδαο is the epic genitive of Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’, Achilles, and βίηφιν has the old ending -φιν in place of a case ending, so ὑπὸ … βίηφιν is ‘under the might’ of Achilles.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ἔθελεν ῥῆξαι στίχας ἀνδρῶν πειρητίζων,
ᾗ δὴ πλεῖστον ὅμιλον ὅρα καὶ τεύχε’ ἄριστα·
sentences.l:
And he wished to break the ranks of men, making trial,
where indeed he saw the thickest throng and the best armour;
sentences.i: He wished to break the ranks of men, testing them, at the place where he saw the thickest throng and the finest armour;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ ἔθελεν: the subject is Hector, and ἔθελεν is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’. ῥῆξαι is the aorist infinitive of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, and στίχας ἀνδρῶν ‘ranks of men’ its object. πειρητίζων is ‘making trial’ of the line. ᾗ δή is ‘where indeed’, and ὅρα is a past tense of ὁράω, ‘saw’, without the augment. πλεῖστον ὅμιλον is ‘the thickest throng’ and τεύχε’ ἄριστα ‘the best armour’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς δύνατο ῥῆξαι μάλα περ μενεαίνων·
sentences.l: but not even so could he break them, though very eager;
sentences.i: But even so he could not break them, however eager he was;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘not even so’, and δύνατο the imperfect middle of δύναμαι ‘be able’. μάλα περ μενεαίνων is ‘though very eager’, with concessive περ and the present participle of μενεαίνω ‘be eager’, a word built on μένος ‘might’. The subject is still Hector, and ῥῆξαι repeats the infinitive of 615.

sentences.t:
ἴσχον γὰρ πυργηδὸν ἀρηρότες, ἠΰτε πέτρη
ἠλίβατος μεγάλη πολιῆς ἁλὸς ἐγγὺς ἐοῦσα,
ἥ τε μένει λιγέων ἀνέμων λαιψηρὰ κέλευθα
κύματά τε τροφόεντα, τά τε προσερεύγεται αὐτήν·
sentences.l:
for they held, tower-fashion, fitted close, like a rock
towering, great, being near the grey sea,
which awaits the quick ways of the clear winds
and the swelling waves, which break against it;
sentences.i: for they held, fitted close together like a tower, like a great, towering rock beside the grey sea, which awaits the quick ways of the clear-sounding winds and the swelling waves that break against it;
sentences.n: ἴσχον is the imperfect of ἴσχω ‘hold’ (their ground), with the subject the Achaeans, and πυργηδόν is ‘like a tower’. ἀρηρότες is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’. ἠΰτε is ‘like’. ἠλίβατος, ‘towering’, is a word whose meaning is not known; ‘towering’ is the traditional guess. πολιῆς ἁλός is ‘the grey sea’. μένει is ‘awaits’, and λιγέων ἀνέμων ‘clear winds’ is the genitive. τροφόεντα is taken as ‘swelling’, a guess from τρέφω. προσερεύγεται is literally ‘belches against’, of a wave breaking on the rock.

sentences.t: ὣς Δαναοὶ Τρῶας μένον ἔμπεδον οὐδὲ φέβοντο.
sentences.l: So the Danaans awaited the Trojans firmly, nor took flight.
sentences.i: So the Danaans awaited the Trojans steadily, and did not take flight.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the simile of the rock: the Danaans are the rock, and as μένει took the winds as its object, μένον takes Τρῶας, ‘awaited’. μένον is the unaugmented imperfect. ἔμπεδον is the adverb of ἔμπεδος ‘firm’, φέβοντο the imperfect middle of φέβομαι ‘take flight’, and οὐδέ ‘and … not’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ λαμπόμενος πυρὶ πάντοθεν ἔνθορ’ ὁμίλῳ,
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ ὡς ὅτε κῦμα θοῇ ἐν νηῒ πέσῃσι
λάβρον ὑπαὶ νεφέων ἀνεμοτρεφές·
sentences.i: But he, gleaming with fire on every side, leapt into the throng and fell upon them, as a wave, fierce and wind-nurtured, falls from beneath the clouds upon a swift ship;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’, Hector. λαμπόμενος πυρί is ‘shining with fire’, the participle of λάμπομαι. ἔνθορ’ is the aorist of ἐνθρῴσκω ‘leap in’, with ὁμίλῳ ‘into the throng’. ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ is ‘fell upon’, the preverb ἐν apart from the verb. ὡς ὅτε κῦμα … πέσῃσι is ‘as when a wave falls’, an aorist subjunctive, on a ship, θοῇ ἐν νηῒ (with the printed diaeresis). λάβρον is ‘fierce’, and ὑπαὶ νεφέων ‘beneath the clouds’. ἀνεμοτρεφές ‘wind-nurtured’ is built from ἄνεμος ‘wind’ and τρέφω ‘nourish’, and the wave is one the wind has fed.

sentences.t:
ἣ δέ τε πᾶσα
ἄχνῃ ὑπεκρύφθη, ἀνέμοιο δὲ δεινὸς ἀήτη
ἱστίῳ ἐμβρέμεται, τρομέουσι δέ τε φρένα ναῦται
δειδιότες·
sentences.l:
and she, all of her,
is hidden beneath the spray, and of the wind the dread blast
roars in the sail, and they tremble in their wits, the sailors,
fearing;
sentences.i: and the whole ship is hidden under the spray, and the dread blast of the wind roars in the sail, and the sailors tremble in their wits, afraid;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ τε πᾶσα is ‘and the whole of it’, the ship. ὑπεκρύφθη is the aorist passive of ὑποκρύπτω ‘hide beneath’, an aorist that states a general fact, ‘is hidden’, with ἄχνῃ ‘spray’ as the dative of means. ἀνέμοιο … ἀήτη is ‘the blast of the wind’, and ἱστίῳ ἐμβρέμεται is ‘roars in the sail’. τρομέουσι is the uncontracted form of τρομέω ‘tremble’, and φρένα an accusative of respect, ‘in their wits’. δειδιότες is the perfect participle of δείδω ‘fear’.

sentences.t: τυτθὸν γὰρ ὑπ’ ἐκ θανάτοιο φέρονται·
sentences.l: for a little from under death they are carried;
sentences.i: for they are carried only a little way out from under death;
sentences.n: τυτθόν ‘a little’ is an adverb, and ὑπ’ ἐκ θανάτοιο ‘from under death’ has both ὑπό and ἐκ with the epic genitive. φέρονται is the present passive, ‘they are carried’. The sense is that the sailors are only just clear of death, and the clause gives the reason (γάρ) for their fear in the line before.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐδαΐζετο θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: So was torn the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans was torn apart.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the picture of the ship: the sailors’ terror is the Achaeans’ terror. ἐδαΐζετο is the imperfect passive of δαΐζω ‘tear apart’, so the heart ‘was torn’. ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is ‘in the breasts’, with the epic dative plural in -εσσι, and Ἀχαιῶν the genitive plural, ‘of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ὥς τε λέων ὀλοόφρων βουσὶν ἐπελθών,
αἵ ῥά τ’ ἐν εἱαμενῇ ἕλεος μεγάλοιο νέμονται
μυρίαι, ἐν δέ τε τῇσι νομεὺς οὔ πω σάφα εἰδὼς
θηρὶ μαχέσσασθαι ἕλικος βοὸς ἀμφὶ φονῇσιν·
sentences.l:
But he, like a lion, baleful-minded, having come upon cattle
that graze in the water-meadow of a great marsh,
countless, and among them a herdsman, not yet clearly knowing
how to fight with a beast about the killing of a crumple-horned ox;
sentences.i: But he was like a baleful-minded lion that has come upon cattle grazing in the water-meadow of a great marsh, countless cattle, and among them a herdsman who does not yet know clearly how to fight a beast over the killing of an ox of crumpled horn;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is Hector again. ὥς τε λέων ὀλοόφρων is ‘like a baleful-minded lion’, ὀλοός ‘deadly’ + φρήν ‘mind’, and βουσὶν ἐπελθών ‘having come upon cattle’. αἵ … νέμονται ‘which graze’ refers to the cattle, and εἱαμενῇ ἕλεος μεγάλοιο is ‘the water-meadow of a great marsh’. μυρίαι is ‘countless’. νομεύς ‘herdsman’ is the man who does not yet know σάφα ‘clearly’ how to fight a beast, μαχέσσασθαι. ἕλικος βοός is ‘of a crumple-horned ox’, as with ἕλικας βοῦς elsewhere, and φονῇσιν is a dative plural, ‘killing’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν πρώτῃσι καὶ ὑστατίῃσι βόεσσιν
αἰὲν ὁμοστιχάει, ὃ δέ τ’ ἐν μέσσῃσιν ὀρούσας
βοῦν ἔδει, αἳ δέ τε πᾶσαι ὑπέτρεσαν·
sentences.i: The herdsman always goes in line with the foremost cows and the hindmost, but the lion springs into the midst of them and devours a cow, and all of them take fright;
sentences.n: ἤτοι ὃ μὲν … ὃ δέ τ’ is ‘the one … the other’: the herdsman, then the lion. πρώτῃσι καὶ ὑστατίῃσι βόεσσιν is ‘beside the first and the last cows’, the epic dative plural in -ῃσι and -εσσι, and ὁμοστιχάει (uncontracted for ὁμοστιχᾷ) is ‘goes in line with’. ἐν μέσσῃσιν ὀρούσας is ‘springing among the middle ones’, and ἔδει is the third singular of ἔδω ‘eat’. ὑπέτρεσαν is the aorist of ὑποτρέω ‘take fright’, from the verb at 586.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
θεσπεσίως ἐφόβηθεν ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι καὶ Διὶ πατρὶ
πάντες,
sentences.l:
so then the Achaeans
wondrously were put to flight under Hector and father Zeus,
all of them,
sentences.i: so the Achaeans, all of them, were wondrously put to flight by Hector and father Zeus,
sentences.n: ὣς τότ’ Ἀχαιοί ‘so then the Achaeans’ closes the simile of the lion. θεσπεσίως is ‘wondrously’, the adverb of θεσπέσιος. ἐφόβηθεν is the aorist passive of φοβέω, ‘were put to flight’, and ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι καὶ Διὶ πατρί puts the cause as ‘under Hector and father Zeus’, the dative with ὑπό; Διὶ πατρί ‘father Zeus’ is a stock phrase. πάντες ‘all of them’ comes after the verb, for emphasis.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οἶον ἔπεφνε Μυκηναῖον Περιφήτην,
Κοπρῆος φίλον υἱόν, ὃς Εὐρυσθῆος ἄνακτος
ἀγγελίης οἴχνεσκε βίῃ Ἡρακληείῃ.
sentences.l:
and he killed one alone, Mycenaean Periphetes,
dear son of Copreus, who, on a message of lord Eurystheus,
used to go to the might of Heracles.
sentences.i: and he killed one man only, Mycenaean Periphetes, the dear son of Copreus, who used to go to the might of Heracles on messages from lord Eurystheus.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is Hector. ἔπεφνε is the aorist of φένω ‘slay’, the verb behind πέφανται at 563. οἶον is accusative, agreeing with Περιφήτην, ‘one alone’; the Greek does not say whether he was alone in the field or simply the only man killed. Κοπρῆος is the epic genitive of Κοπρεύς, and φίλον υἱόν is ‘dear son’. οἴχνεσκε is the iterative imperfect of οἴχνεω ‘go’, ‘used to go’. Εὐρυσθῆος ἄνακτος ἀγγελίης is ‘on the message of lord Eurystheus’, and βίῃ Ἡρακληείῃ ‘to the might of Heracles’ is a periphrasis for Heracles himself.

sentences.t:
τοῦ γένετ’ ἐκ πατρὸς πολὺ χείρονος υἱὸς ἀμείνων
παντοίας ἀρετάς, ἠμὲν πόδας ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι,
καὶ νόον ἐν πρώτοισι Μυκηναίων ἐτέτυκτο·
sentences.i: From that father, a far worse man, was born a better son, in every kind of excellence, both in speed of foot and in fighting, and in mind; he was made one of the first among the Mycenaeans;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of him’ is Copreus, and ἐκ πατρὸς πολὺ χείρονος ‘from a much worse father’ restates him as the father, with χείρων the comparative of κακός. υἱὸς ἀμείνων ‘a better son’ is Periphetes. παντοίας ἀρετάς is an accusative of respect, ‘in every kind of excellence’ (ἀρετή), and ἠμὲν … ἠδὲ is ‘both … and’, πόδας ‘in feet’ and μάχεσθαι ‘in fighting’. καὶ νόον adds ‘and in mind’. ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’: ‘he had been made’ among the first of the Mycenaeans.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα τόθ’ Ἕκτορι κῦδος ὑπέρτερον ἐγγυάλιξε.
sentences.l: who then to Hector greater glory put into his hands.
sentences.i: It was he who then put greater glory into the hands of Hector.
sentences.n: ὅς ῥα τόθ’ is ‘who then’, and ὅς is Periphetes. ἐγγυάλιξε is the aorist of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands of’, with Ἕκτορι the dative of the person. κῦδος ὑπέρτερον is ‘greater glory’. The next lines say how: he tripped and fell, and Hector killed him.

sentences.t:
στρεφθεὶς γὰρ μετόπισθεν ἐν ἀσπίδος ἄντυγι πάλτο,
τὴν αὐτὸς φορέεσκε ποδηνεκέ’ ἕρκος ἀκόντων·
sentences.l:
for, having turned backward, on the rim of the shield he stumbled,
which he himself kept carrying, reaching to the feet, a fence against javelins;
sentences.i: for as he turned back he stumbled on the rim of the shield that he himself carried, a shield reaching to his feet, a bulwark against javelins;
sentences.n: στρεφθείς is the aorist passive participle of στρέφω ‘turn’, and μετόπισθεν ‘backward’. ἐν ἀσπίδος ἄντυγι πάλτο: ἄντυξ is the ‘rim’ of the shield, and πάλτο is the aorist middle of πάλλω ‘swing’; with ἐν its exact sense is debated (‘struck against’, ‘stumbled’), and ‘stumbled’ fits the next line. τὴν αὐτὸς φορέεσκε is ‘which he himself kept carrying’, φορέεσκε an iterative imperfect of φορέω. ποδηνεκέ’ is ‘reaching to the feet’, agreeing with τήν, and ἕρκος ἀκόντων is ‘a fence against javelins’.

sentences.t:
τῇ ὅ γ’ ἐνὶ βλαφθεὶς πέσεν ὕπτιος, ἀμφὶ δὲ πήληξ
σμερδαλέον κονάβησε περὶ κροτάφοισι πεσόντος.
sentences.l:
On it he, hindered, fell on his back, and the helmet about him
terribly rang about the temples of him as he fell.
sentences.i: Hindered by it, he fell on his back, and the helmet rang terribly about his temples as he fell.
sentences.n: τῇ … ἐνί is ‘on it’, the rim, with ἐνί (= ἐν) set after the pronoun and ὅ γ’ between. βλαφθείς is the aorist passive participle of βλάπτω ‘hinder’, and ὕπτιος ‘on his back’. πήληξ is the helmet, as at 608, and σμερδαλέον ‘terribly’ is also as at 609. κονάβησε is the aorist of κοναβέω ‘ring’, and πεσόντος, the aorist participle in the genitive, is ‘of him as he fell’, after κροτάφοισι ‘temples’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὀξὺ νόησε, θέων δέ οἱ ἄγχι παρέστη,
στήθεϊ δ’ ἐν δόρυ πῆξε, φίλων δέ μιν ἐγγὺς ἑταίρων
κτεῖν’·
sentences.i: Hector was quick to notice it, and ran up and stood close beside him, and fixed his spear in his chest, and killed him there, close to his dear companions;
sentences.n: ὀξὺ νόησε is ‘sharply noticed’: ὀξύ is an adverb and νόησε the aorist of νοέω. θέων is ‘running’, οἱ ‘to him’, and ἄγχι παρέστη ‘stood close beside’. στήθεϊ δ’ ἐν δόρυ πῆξε is ‘fixed his spear in his chest’, with ἐν apart from πῆξε and the dative στήθεϊ. φίλων … ἐγγὺς ἑταίρων is ‘near his dear companions’, with ἐγγύς taking the genitive, and κτεῖν’ is κτεῖνε ‘killed’, elided.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ οὐκ ἐδύναντο καὶ ἀχνύμενοί περ ἑταίρου
χραισμεῖν·
sentences.l:
and they were not able, though grieving for their companion,
to help;
sentences.i: but they could not help him, grieving though they were for their companion;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ is ‘they’, the companions of Periphetes. ἐδύναντο is the imperfect of δύναμαι ‘be able’, and ἀχνύμενοί περ ‘though grieving’ is a participle of ἄχνυμαι with concessive περ. ἑταίρου is the genitive ‘for their companion’, going with ἀχνύμενοι. χραισμεῖν is the aorist infinitive of χραισμέω ‘help’, with no object in the Greek.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ γὰρ μάλα δείδισαν Ἕκτορα δῖον.
sentences.l: for they themselves greatly feared heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: for they were very much afraid of heavenly Hector themselves.
sentences.n: αὐτοὶ γάρ gives the reason, ‘for they themselves’, set against the grief of the line before. δείδισαν is a past tense of δείδω ‘fear’, and μάλα ‘greatly’. Ἕκτορα δῖον is the stock phrase ‘heavenly Hector’, with δῖος translated the same way every time, even of the man they fear.
